restart_api_pool.detail: Rolling restart dropped failures to about 18% for 40 seconds; the pool refilled on the same v2.18.1 build and the incident returned.
restart_api_pool.lesson: Restarting payment-api again produced a 40 second dip and then regression - the second time, the previous incident's lesson was already in memory.
restart_api_pool.reusable_lesson: Second confirmation: restarting payment-api workers during a Redis pool exhaustion incident is a temporary mitigation (5xx 14% -> 5% for ~40s) followed by regression to 24%. Stop retrying it and go to the pool diagnostic or rollback.
restart_api_pool.warning: Previous similar incident: restarting API pods produced only temporary improvement and regression.

rollback_recent_deploy.detail: Rolled back to v2.18.0 and raised the client pool to 200. Failures cleared within 3 minutes, pool at 71/200, no 502/503.
rollback_recent_deploy.lesson: Rollback of the release that touched the client lifecycle resolved the second occurrence too.
rollback_recent_deploy.reusable_lesson: Rolling back the release that changed the checkout client lifecycle resolved payment-api Redis pool exhaustion in both INC-A1 and INC-A2; confirm the suspect release with the deploy diff before rolling back.

increase_redis_pool_size.detail: Raising the client pool from 150 to 200 with a 250ms acquisition timeout cleared the backlog, but the leak is still shipping - flagged as a mitigation with a follow-up required.
increase_redis_pool_size.lesson: More headroom bought time; the leak remains and will recur (third occurrence already predicted by the service pattern).
increase_redis_pool_size.reusable_lesson: Raising the payment-api client pool clears a Redis pool exhaustion incident temporarily, but as long as the leaking release is deployed the pool saturates again - always pair it with a rollback or a leak fix.

scale_out_workers.detail: Scaling out doubled the connection demand: 150 per worker against a Redis maxclients ceiling, failures rose to 26%.
scale_out_workers.lesson: Per-worker pool sizing means scaling out accelerates pool exhaustion.
scale_out_workers.reusable_lesson: Do not scale payment-api out to fight a Redis pool exhaustion incident: the client pool is per worker, so more workers exhaust the shared Redis faster (INC-A1 and INC-A2 both made this worse).

isolate_dependency.detail: Isolating the PSP dependency had no measurable effect on failures: the cache pool, not the PSP, is blocking the checkout path. It does reduce retry amplification (PSP retries 640 -> 90).
isolate_dependency.lesson: Degraded PSP latency was a real distractor: isolating it reduced retries but not failures.
isolate_dependency.reusable_lesson: In payment-api checkout incidents, an elevated PSP latency can be a distractor - isolating the PSP reduces retry load but does not change the failure rate when the client Redis pool is saturated.

flush_cache.detail: High-risk action: a cart cache flush would destroy in-flight checkouts and raise duplicate-charge risk. Blocked by the safety gate by default.
flush_cache.lesson: Destructive and pointless for a client-side pool leak.
flush_cache.reusable_lesson: Never flush the payment-api cart cache as remediation: it destroys in-flight checkout state and does not fix a client-side connection leak.
